title: How America Doubled in Size for 3 Cents an Acre
hook: In 1803 an American diplomat asked France for one city and was offered a territory nearly as big as his whole country, for about three cents an acre.
thumbnail_picture: Close on the right: a stunned young American explorer in 1804 buckskin and a wide hat stands on a grassy bluff, mouth open, staring at an endless golden prairie with huge bison herds under a blazing sunset sky. Left third empty sky.
description:
How America roughly doubled in size for 3 cents an acre: the true story of the 1803 Louisiana Purchase, from Jefferson's New Orleans problem to Napoleon's surprise offer and Lewis and Clark.
Why did Napoleon sell Louisiana? Yellow fever and Haitian resistance, a coming war with Britain, and a president who wasn't sure the Constitution allowed the deal.

Sources and further reading:
- Louisiana Purchase Treaty (1803), U.S. National Archives
- "Jefferson's Great Gamble" by Charles A. Cerami
- "Undaunted Courage" by Stephen E. Ambrose
- Monticello (Thomas Jefferson Foundation), Louisiana Purchase and Lewis and Clark resources

scenes.narration: Paris, April 1803. An American diplomat has spent months begging France to sell him one city. Then he's offered a territory nearly as big as his whole country.
scenes.delivery: hushed, urgent, like the start of a thriller
scenes.picture: Robert Livingston, weary middle-aged American diplomat with gray hair, dark coat and white cravat, sits frozen in a gilded Paris office, eyes wide in shock, a quill slipping from his fingers, a French official in a dark embroidered coat leaning toward him across the desk, candlelight.

scenes.narration: The price? About three cents an acre. But back home, the president who sent him isn't sure buying it is even legal.
scenes.caption: 3 CENTS AN ACRE
scenes.picture: Thomas Jefferson, tall thin 60-year-old man with red-gray hair and a plain dark coat, paces alone in a candlelit 1803 study, one hand on his chin, worried frown, a quill and blank paper on the wooden desk beside him.

scenes.narration: So why would Napoleon, the most powerful man in Europe, sell it all so cheap? The answer starts with a mosquito.
scenes.delivery: curious, teasing, a beat before the last word
scenes.caption: THE DEAL
scenes.picture: Napoleon Bonaparte, short stern man in a dark blue military coat with gold epaulettes and a black bicorne hat, stands with arms crossed staring down at a single tiny mosquito resting on the back of his white glove, dim palace room, close-up.

scenes.narration: It starts with a Kentucky farmer loading flour onto a flatboat. Everything he owns floats south toward one port: New Orleans.
scenes.caption: KENTUCKY
scenes.picture: A Kentucky farmer in a homespun shirt and straw hat loads flour barrels onto a flat wooden boat at a muddy riverbank at dawn, mist on the water.

scenes.narration: The Mississippi was America's highway. Mountain roads were awful, so New Orleans was Western farmers' main outlet to the world.
scenes.caption: THE MAIN DOOR
scenes.picture: Wide view of the broad Mississippi River with many flatboats and keelboats drifting downstream between green forested banks, midday sun, 1800s.

scenes.narration: But whoever held New Orleans could slam that door. Spain held it, and under a 1795 treaty, it let Americans store their goods there.
scenes.caption: WHO HOLDS THE KEY
scenes.picture: A heavy iron key held in a hand in the foreground, with a busy 1802 New Orleans port behind it: wooden docks, ships, and Spanish-style balconies, warm afternoon light.

scenes.narration: Then Jefferson got news that changed everything. By 1802, he'd learned Spain had secretly agreed to hand New Orleans, and all of Louisiana, back to France.
scenes.caption: A SECRET DEAL
scenes.picture: Thomas Jefferson, tall thin 60-year-old man with red-gray hair and a plain dark coat, reads a letter with a shocked face, one hand on his forehead, candle and quill beside him, evening 1803 study.

scenes.narration: France meant Napoleon. He'd just made peace in Europe, so he dreamed of a new French empire across the Atlantic.
scenes.caption: NAPOLEON
scenes.picture: Napoleon Bonaparte, short man with brown hair in a dark blue uniform with gold trim, stands at a tall palace window with hands behind his back, gazing out proudly, Paris 1802.

scenes.narration: So Jefferson wrote a blunt letter to his man in Paris. If France takes New Orleans, he said, America must side with Britain.
scenes.caption: JEFFERSON WORRIES
scenes.picture: Close-up of a hand writing quickly with a quill pen on paper, an ink bottle and a stick of red sealing wax beside it, dim candlelight, 1802 desk.

scenes.narration: Jefferson didn't even like Britain. That's how worried he was.
scenes.caption: HOW WORRIED?
scenes.picture: Thomas Jefferson, tall thin 60-year-old man with red-gray hair and a plain dark coat, sits alone at a night desk with a stormy troubled face, his big shadow looming on the wall behind him.

scenes.narration: So he sent James Monroe across the Atlantic with permission to spend up to ten million dollars.
scenes.caption: MONROE SAILS
scenes.picture: James Monroe, serious tall man with brown hair in a dark coat and tricorn hat, stands on the deck of a sailing ship as it leaves an American harbor, wind blowing his coat.

scenes.narration: The goal was small: New Orleans and the Floridas. A whole territory wasn't the plan.
scenes.caption: A SMALL GOAL
scenes.picture: A single busy river port city, New Orleans 1802, with brick warehouses, a levee and a few ships tied up on a bend of a wide river, small and modest, afternoon sun.

scenes.narration: But the real turning point wasn't in Paris or Washington. It was on a Caribbean island, in the jungle.
scenes.caption: THE TWIST
scenes.picture: A lush green jungle hillside on a tropical Caribbean island with palm trees and a distant blue bay, humid mist, dramatic light, 1802.

scenes.narration: Louisiana was meant to feed Saint-Domingue, France's sugar colony, now Haiti. But formerly enslaved people there had risen up and seized control.
scenes.caption: HAITI
scenes.picture: Haitian fighters, men and women in simple 1800s clothes with muskets, stand on a hill above sugarcane fields at sunset, determined faces, Saint-Domingue 1802.

scenes.narration: So Napoleon sent tens of thousands of soldiers to take it back. Their leader was his own brother-in-law.
scenes.caption: AN ARMY SAILS
scenes.picture: A fleet of French warships anchored in a tropical bay while soldiers in blue coats row ashore in small boats, hazy morning, Saint-Domingue 1802.

scenes.narration: But they were met by fighters who knew the land, and by something worse: yellow fever.
scenes.caption: FEVER
scenes.picture: A swarm of mosquitoes glowing in the humid dusk air above a swampy tropical camp with canvas tents and campfires, foreboding mood, 1802.

scenes.narration: Mosquitoes carried it. Soldiers burned with fever and died by the thousands. The general himself caught it and died.
scenes.caption: THOUSANDS DIE
scenes.picture: A French army officer in a blue coat lies pale and sweating on a camp bed inside a canvas tent, a worried soldier leaning over him, dim oil lamp, 1802.

scenes.narration: Tens of thousands of French soldiers never came home. So Napoleon's American empire had nobody left to defend it.
scenes.caption: THE ARMY VANISHES
scenes.picture: A long line of simple wooden crosses on a tropical hillside at dusk, with one young French drummer boy in a blue coat walking away alone, sad mood.

scenes.narration: And he had another problem: he expected a new war with Britain, and it came just a month later. Britain's navy could grab Louisiana whenever it wanted.
scenes.caption: BRITAIN LOOMS
scenes.picture: A line of big British warships with many sails sailing in formation across a gray stormy sea, menacing, wide view, 1803.

scenes.narration: So Napoleon needed cash, and he couldn't defend a land he could barely reach. He made a decision that dismayed some of his own circle.
scenes.caption: A BIG DECISION
scenes.picture: Napoleon Bonaparte, short man with brown hair in a dark blue uniform with gold trim, leans over a large desk piled with gold coins, stern calculating face, candlelit Paris palace room.

scenes.narration: Paris, spring of 1803. Robert Livingston, America's minister, had been begging for New Orleans for months.
scenes.caption: PARIS, 1803
scenes.picture: Robert Livingston, weary middle-aged American diplomat with gray hair, dark coat and white cravat, walks alone along a Paris cobblestone street with horse carriages, spring day, tired face.

scenes.narration: Nobody in the French government would even talk to him. Then, on April 11, a diplomat named Talleyrand asked a strange question.
scenes.caption: APRIL 11
scenes.picture: Talleyrand, elegant French man with powdered hair and a fine plum coat, smiles slyly across a polished table at a surprised American diplomat in a gilded Paris office, 1803.

scenes.narration: What would America give for the whole of Louisiana? Livingston was stunned.
scenes.caption: THE WHOLE THING?
scenes.picture: Close-up of Robert Livingston, weary middle-aged man with gray hair and white cravat, with wide shocked eyes and raised eyebrows, mouth slightly open, gilded office behind him.

scenes.narration: The whole thing? He only had orders to buy a city, and nowhere near that kind of money.
scenes.caption: NO ORDERS
scenes.picture: An empty brown leather money pouch turned upside down in a man's hand, nothing falling out, with a blurred worried man in a dark coat behind it, 1803.

scenes.narration: Then Monroe's ship landed, and two Americans sat down to bargain with Napoleon's finance minister, Barbé-Marbois.
scenes.caption: THE NEGOTIATION
scenes.picture: Three men in 1800s coats lean toward each other around a candlelit table in a Paris townhouse, two Americans and one Frenchman in a gray wig, serious bargaining faces.

scenes.narration: France's first ask was much higher. So the Americans haggled, day after day, in a stuffy Paris office.
scenes.caption: HAGGLING
scenes.picture: A stuffy Paris office in 1803: a sweating American diplomat in a dark coat raises one hand in protest across a cluttered table with quill pens, an open window behind him.

scenes.narration: At last they settled on fifteen million dollars. For that, they got land bigger than modern France, Spain, Germany and the UK combined.
scenes.caption: $15 MILLION
scenes.picture: An enormous green prairie under a huge sky with a river winding through it, seen from high above, wild and untouched, golden light, 1803.

scenes.narration: According to Barbé-Marbois, Napoleon reportedly said he'd just handed Britain a rival that would one day humble its pride.
scenes.caption: NAPOLEON'S BET
scenes.picture: Napoleon Bonaparte, short man with brown hair in a dark blue uniform, stands on a palace balcony at dusk with one hand tucked in his coat and a small proud smile, Paris rooftops behind.

scenes.narration: The treaty is dated April 30, 1803. Livingston reportedly said, we have lived long, but this is the noblest work of our whole lives.
scenes.caption: APRIL 30, 1803
scenes.picture: Robert Livingston, gray-haired man in a dark coat, and James Monroe, tall brown-haired man in a dark coat, shake hands over a table with a signed treaty, smiling with relief, golden candlelight.

scenes.narration: But they'd had no permission to buy anything close to that. They signed anyway, and sent the news home by ship.
scenes.caption: NO PERMISSION
scenes.picture: A courier in a dark coat and tricorn hat hurries up a ship's gangplank carrying a leather satchel at a French harbor at dawn, gulls overhead, 1803.

scenes.narration: Then the news sailed west: about two months on a wooden ship, while Jefferson waited.
scenes.caption: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC
scenes.picture: A lone wooden sailing ship tossed on big gray-green Atlantic waves under a stormy sky, sails full of wind, medium-wide shot.

scenes.narration: It reached Washington on the eve of July 4, just in time for Independence Day.
scenes.caption: JULY 1803
scenes.picture: A crowd of ordinary 1803 Americans in a small muddy Washington street cheers and tosses hats in the air, a rider on a horse in the middle, Fourth of July, sunny.

scenes.narration: Jefferson should've been thrilled. Instead, he was worried, because the Constitution says nothing about buying land from another country.
scenes.caption: THE PROBLEM
scenes.picture: Thomas Jefferson, tall thin man with red-gray hair and a plain dark coat, sits in a candlelit study with his chin on his hand, staring into the flame with a deeply troubled face, evening.

scenes.narration: He was the one who'd always argued government can only do what the Constitution allows. Now he was stretching it himself.
scenes.caption: JEFFERSON'S DILEMMA
scenes.picture: Thomas Jefferson, tall man with red-gray hair and dark coat, and James Madison, small man with receding gray hair and black coat, argue quietly beside a window in a 1803 room, Madison pointing.

scenes.narration: So he drafted an amendment to fix it. But his advisers said no: wait, and Napoleon might change his mind.
scenes.caption: WAIT OR ACT?
scenes.picture: An old brass pocket clock ticking on a wooden desk beside a quill pen, a candle burning low, two blurred worried men's shadows on the wall behind, close-up.

scenes.narration: Napoleon was famous for changing his mind. So Jefferson dropped the amendment and pushed the treaty through.
scenes.caption: HE CHOOSES
scenes.picture: Thomas Jefferson, tall man with red-gray hair and a plain dark coat, crumples a draft paper in his fist and pushes it aside, determined face, wooden desk in a 1803 study.

scenes.narration: The Senate voted on October 20, 1803: twenty-four to seven in favor. America had bought a territory nobody had really seen.
scenes.caption: OCTOBER 20
scenes.picture: Senators in 1803 coats and white cravats sit in a small plain chamber, many raising their hands in a vote, afternoon light through tall windows.

scenes.narration: But critics screamed. Federalists, especially in New England, called it a waste of money on a wilderness.
scenes.caption: THE CRITICS
scenes.picture: Angry gentlemen in tall hats and dark 1803 coats shake fists at each other on a Boston brick street, red faces, blurred crowd behind them.

scenes.narration: In New Orleans, on December 20, 1803, the French flag came down and the American flag went up.
scenes.caption: NEW ORLEANS
scenes.picture: Soldiers in blue uniforms stand at attention in a sunny New Orleans square as a flag is lowered from a tall pole and another is raised, blurred crowd watching, 1803.

scenes.narration: Many people watching spoke French or Spanish, and wondered what being American would mean for them.
scenes.caption: NEW CITIZENS
scenes.picture: Close shot of onlookers in colorful early 1800s French and Spanish colonial clothes watching a ceremony in a New Orleans square, uncertain curious faces.

scenes.narration: But here's the strange part. Jefferson had just bought it, and he had no idea what he'd bought.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID HE BUY?
scenes.picture: Thomas Jefferson, tall thin man with red-gray hair and a plain dark coat, gazes out a tall window toward a distant western horizon of wild land with a puzzled hopeful smile, afternoon light.

scenes.narration: Nobody did. Jefferson half hoped for mountains of salt, and maybe even giant ice-age beasts still roaming the West.
scenes.caption: MASTODONS?
scenes.picture: An American mastodon, a shaggy dark-brown elephant-like animal with long curved tusks, standing on a misty grassy plain at sunrise, glowing dreamlike light.

scenes.narration: So he'd already picked someone to find out: his secretary, Meriwether Lewis. Lewis chose his friend William Clark.
scenes.caption: LEWIS AND CLARK
scenes.picture: Meriwether Lewis, young dark-haired man in a buckskin jacket and wide hat, and William Clark, red-haired man in a buckskin jacket and wide hat, shake hands grinning beside a boat on a riverbank, 1804.

scenes.narration: In May 1804, their boats pushed off near St. Louis and turned up the Missouri River.
scenes.caption: MAY 1804
scenes.picture: A big keelboat with a square sail and two smaller wooden canoes leaving a muddy riverbank near St. Louis, men waving, spring morning, wide view, 1804.

scenes.narration: But the river fought back. They hauled the heavy boat upstream against the current, dragging it with ropes, day after day.
scenes.caption: UPSTREAM
scenes.picture: A line of sweating men in buckskin pulling a heavy rope along a muddy Missouri riverbank, hauling a keelboat against the current, hot sun.

scenes.narration: Along the way, they met nations who'd lived here for thousands of years. The land had never been empty.
scenes.caption: NATIVE NATIONS
scenes.picture: Native American villagers outside round earth lodges on a grassy Missouri riverbank, welcoming two explorers in buckskin with calm faces, afternoon light.

scenes.narration: That's what the treaty glossed over. France had sold its claim to the land, not the people already living on it.
scenes.caption: WHOSE LAND?
scenes.picture: A Native American elder in a feathered robe stands alone on a grassy hill at sunset, looking over a wide river valley, calm and dignified.

scenes.narration: Winter came at a Mandan village in what's now North Dakota. There, a teenage Shoshone woman named Sacagawea joined them.
scenes.caption: SACAGAWEA
scenes.picture: Sacagawea, young Shoshone woman with long black braids, buckskin dress and a baby on her back, stands in snow beside a log fort, bundled in furs, calm determined face, winter 1804.

scenes.narration: Then the prairie stretched on forever. The explorers' journals describe herds of bison covering the plains as far as they could see.
scenes.caption: BISON
scenes.picture: Vast herds of bison cover a golden prairie to the horizon, with a few tiny explorers on a rise watching them, big sky, late afternoon, 1805.

scenes.narration: They even shipped Jefferson a live prairie dog. It survived the trip to the President's House.
scenes.caption: A PRAIRIE DOG
scenes.picture: A small prairie dog sitting upright in a wooden cage with a surprised look on a table in a grand 1805 room, Thomas Jefferson with red-gray hair smiling behind it.

scenes.narration: Then came the Rocky Mountains: snow in September, empty stomachs, and horses slipping on icy trails.
scenes.caption: THE ROCKIES
scenes.picture: A line of tired explorers in buckskin leads slipping horses along a steep snowy mountain trail through pine trees, cold gray sky, breath misting, 1805.

scenes.narration: But the Shoshone, Sacagawea's own people, traded them horses. Without those horses, the crossing would have been far harder.
scenes.caption: HELP ARRIVES
scenes.picture: A Shoshone chief in a feathered headdress and Meriwether Lewis, dark-haired man in buckskin and wide hat, meet beside a mountain stream, a herd of horses behind them, sunny valley.

scenes.narration: In November 1805, they reached the Pacific Ocean, far beyond the land America had bought.
scenes.caption: THE PACIFIC
scenes.picture: Tired buckskin-clad explorers stand on a stormy Pacific coast beach looking at huge waves rolling in, joy on their faces, cloudy sky, November 1805.

scenes.narration: They came home in September 1806, after about eight thousand miles. Some Americans feared they had been lost.
scenes.caption: HOME AGAIN
scenes.picture: Meriwether Lewis, dark-haired man, and William Clark, red-haired man, in worn buckskin step off a boat toward a cheering blurred crowd on the St. Louis riverbank, sunny day, 1806.

scenes.narration: So what had America really bought? Grasslands, great rivers, mountains, and a future that would fill with farms and towns.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: A wooden covered wagon with a pioneer family crosses a golden prairie toward distant mountains at sunrise, wide sweeping view, 1840.

scenes.narration: Today that one deal covers all or part of fifteen states, from Louisiana to Montana, Oklahoma to Minnesota.
scenes.caption: 15 STATES
scenes.picture: A huge modern wheat field at golden sunset with a combine harvester working on the Great Plains, endless horizon, warm light.

scenes.narration: And it all happened because fever and Haitian fighters wrecked an army, Napoleon needed cash for a war, and a president wanted just one city.
scenes.caption: WHY IT HAPPENED
scenes.picture: Close-up on a wooden table: a small toy mosquito, a pile of gold coins and a tiny model riverboat lined up side by side, warm lamplight.

scenes.narration: Jefferson asked for a door and got the whole house. And that legal worry? Courts later accepted that the country could do it.
scenes.caption: A DOOR AND A HOUSE
scenes.picture: Thomas Jefferson, tall thin man with red-gray hair and a plain dark coat, stands on the front step of a big grand brick house holding one small door key, puzzled amused face, evening light.

scenes.narration: The map of America was redrawn by a fever, a bargain, and a treaty. Not bad for three cents an acre.
scenes.caption: 3 CENTS AN ACRE
scenes.picture: Wide sunrise view over a giant river valley and prairie with a single tiny covered wagon crossing it, glowing orange sky, peaceful.

narrator: Adventurous travel-documentary narrator, energetic and warm, a sense of motion and discovery.

short.title: How America Doubled in Size for 3 Cents an Acre
short.description: In 1803, America bought the Louisiana Territory from Napoleon and doubled in size. Here is the story of how fever, a war and one worried president made it happen. Sources: Library of Congress, National Archives, Monticello (Thomas Jefferson Foundation).

scenes.narration: In 1803, America roughly doubled in size for three cents an acre, so why did France sell?
scenes.picture: Huge close-up of a farmer's open palm holding three copper coins, a vast green American prairie stretching behind it to the horizon, bright morning light, awed mood

scenes.narration: President Thomas Jefferson only wanted New Orleans, the port Western farmers needed.
scenes.caption: NEW ORLEANS
scenes.picture: Close-up of President Thomas Jefferson, tall and red-haired in a plain dark coat, pointing at the port of New Orleans on a map, thoughtful face, candlelit study, 1802

scenes.narration: But France's ruler Napoleon was taking over Louisiana, so Jefferson sent James Monroe to Paris.
scenes.caption: MONROE SAILS
scenes.picture: Close-up of James Monroe, a serious man in a dark coat and tricorn hat, standing on the deck of a sailing ship leaving a harbor, wind in his coat

scenes.narration: Napoleon had sent an army to crush a revolt in Haiti.
scenes.caption: HAITI
scenes.picture: French soldiers in blue coats rowing ashore from warships toward a tropical Haitian bay, Napoleon's army arriving, hazy morning, large close boats

scenes.narration: But yellow fever killed thousands of French soldiers, including their general.
scenes.caption: YELLOW FEVER
scenes.picture: A pale sweating French army officer in a blue coat lying in a camp bed inside a tent, a worried soldier beside him, mosquitoes in the dim lamplight, close-up

scenes.narration: Now France couldn't defend Louisiana, and war with Britain loomed.
scenes.caption: WAR LOOMS
scenes.picture: Close view of big British warships with full sails cutting through a gray stormy sea, menacing, dramatic clouds

scenes.narration: So French diplomat Talleyrand shocked American envoy Robert Livingston by offering all of Louisiana.
scenes.caption: THE OFFER
scenes.picture: Close-up of American diplomat Robert Livingston with wide shocked eyes and open mouth, across a polished table from sly Talleyrand in a fine coat, gilded Paris office, 1803

scenes.narration: Livingston and Monroe haggled, then settled on fifteen million dollars.
scenes.caption: $15 MILLION
scenes.picture: Two American diplomats in 1800s coats shaking hands over a signed treaty paper at a candlelit table in a Paris townhouse, relieved smiles, close shot

scenes.narration: For that, America got roughly 530 million acres.
scenes.caption: 530M ACRES
scenes.picture: An enormous golden prairie under a huge sky with a river winding through it, seen from low above, wild and untouched, glowing light

scenes.narration: Jefferson doubted the Constitution allowed the purchase, but the Senate approved.
scenes.caption: THE SENATE
scenes.picture: Close-up of Jefferson with chin on hand, troubled face, staring at a thick book on a candlelit desk, and behind him senators in 1803 coats raising hands in a vote

scenes.narration: So America roughly doubled in size because yellow fever wrecked Napoleon's army and he needed cash.
scenes.caption: WHY IT HAPPENED
scenes.picture: A tiny covered wagon crossing a golden prairie toward distant mountains at sunrise, big glowing sky, peaceful, large foreground grass
